summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where the last two factors are prime. Writing \(b(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma_1(d)\), multiplicativity and \(a(n)=2\sigma_1(n)-b(n)\), together with \(\sigma_1(2^{14})=32767\), \(b(2^{14})=65519\), and the prime-factor formulas, gives \(a(n)=2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010-65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=1\), although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency of \(m\) is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so the sequence in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Define a second divisor sum
\[
B(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Since \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=\sigma(n)\), separating the two terms in the definition of \(a(n)\) gives the useful identity
\[
\boxed{a(n)=2\sigma(n)-B(n).}
\tag{1}
\]

We will also use the multiplicativity of both \(\sigma\) and \(B\). Here is the argument. If \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, every divisor of \(rs\) is uniquely of the form \(uv\), where \(u\mid r\) and \(v\mid s\). Moreover, \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime. Applying this divisor bijection first to \(\sigma\) gives
\[
\sigma(rs)=\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}uv
 =\left(\sum_{u\mid r}u\right)\left(\sum_{v\mid s}v\right)
 =\sigma(r)\sigma(s).
\tag{2}
\]
Thus \(\sigma\) is multiplicative. Applying the same divisor bijection to \(B\), and then using (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(rs)
 &=\sum_{w\mid rs}\sigma(w)
 =\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)
 =B(r)B(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]
Therefore \(B\) is multiplicative as well.

The counterexample is
\[
N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\tag{4}
\]
The multiplication in (4) is direct: \(2^{14}=16384\), and
\[
16384\cdot 4409\cdot 458009=33085221781504.
\]
The two odd factors \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. For completeness, their primality can be established by the following compact finite certificates.

We use this elementary primality criterion. Suppose the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known. If there is an integer \(c\) such that
\[
c^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(c^{(m-1)/q}-1,m\bigr)=1,
\tag{5}
\]
then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(m\), and let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(c\) modulo \(r\). The first congruence implies \(t\mid m-1\), while (5) implies, for each prime \(q\mid m-1\), that \(t\nmid (m-1)/q\). Hence \(t\) contains the full power of every prime appearing in \(m-1\), so \(m-1\mid t\). On the other hand, Fermat's theorem gives \(t\mid r-1\). Thus \(m-1\mid r-1\), and consequently \(r\ge m\). Since \(r\mid m\), this forces \(r=m\), proving that \(m\) is prime.

Starting from the elementary primes \(2\) and \(3\), the criterion applies recursively using the following data. In each row, the displayed factorization is the complete factorization of \(m-1\); the entry \(R_q\) is the residue of \(c^{(m-1)/q}\) modulo \(m\). In every row, direct repeated-squaring also gives \(c^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m\), and the Euclidean algorithm gives \(\gcd(R_q-1,m)=1\) for every listed \(q\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m & m-1 & c & \text{residues }R_q\text{ for the distinct primes }q\mid m-1\\ \hline
5 & 2^2 & 2 & R_2=4\\
7 & 2\cdot3 & 3 & R_2=6,\ R_3=2\\
19 & 2\cdot3^2 & 2 & R_2=18,\ R_3=7\\
29 & 2^2\cdot7 & 2 & R_2=28,\ R_7=16\\
229 & 2^2\cdot3\cdot19 & 6 & R_2=228,\ R_3=134,\ R_{19}=165\\
57251 & 2\cdot5^3\cdot229 & 2 & R_2=57250,\ R_5=55371,\ R_{229}=48088\\
4409 & 2^3\cdot19\cdot29 & 3 & R_2=4408,\ R_{19}=209,\ R_{29}=3965\\
458009 & 2^3\cdot57251 & 3 & R_2=458008,\ R_{57251}=6561
\end{array}
\]

All arithmetic in this table consists only of modular exponentiation and the Euclidean algorithm. The rows are ordered so that all prime factors needed in a row have already been shown prime in earlier rows. Thus the criterion proves successively that \(5,7,19,29,229,57251,4409\), and \(458009\) are prime. In particular, it establishes the two primality facts needed for (4).

Because \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct odd primes, the three integers \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime. We may therefore apply (2) and (3) repeatedly.

We now calculate the required values on the three prime-power factors. The divisors of \(2^{14}\) are \(2^i\) for \(0\le i\le14\), so
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\tag{6}
\]
For each \(i\ge0\),
\[
\sigma(2^i)=1+2+\cdots+2^i=2^{i+1}-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15}\right)-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15=65519.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Consequently,
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1
\quad\text{and}\quad
B(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\tag{8}
\]
Applying (8) to the two odd prime factors yields
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
p&\sigma(p)&B(p)\\ \hline
4409&4410&4411\\
458009&458010&458011.
\end{array}
\tag{9}
\]

Using multiplicativity, equations (6)--(9) give
\[
\sigma(N)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
	ag{10}
\]
and
\[
B(N)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\tag{11}
\]
For clarity, the two resulting integer products are
\[
32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700
	ag{12}
\]
and
\[
65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=132367152569399.
	ag{13}
\]
Substitution into (1) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-B(N)\\
 &=2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
   -65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, \(N=33085221781504>12\), so \(N\ne1\) and \(N\ne12\). Thus \(a(N)=1\), while the assertion \(N=1\) or \(N=12\) is false. This counterexample disproves the claimed biconditional that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
